[2021 summer phd math-stat — problem 2]

Consider the following regression problem. Let $y_1, \dots, y_n$ be jointly normal with $\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta x_i$, where $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are known constants, $\operatorname{var}(y_i) = \sigma^2$, and $\operatorname{corr}(y_i, y_j) = \rho$ for $i \ne j$. The parameters satisfy $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma^2 > 0$, and $-1/(n-1) < \rho < 1$.

Useful linear-algebra fact: for $I_n$ the identity, $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and $b \ne -1/(a^T a)$, $(I_n + b\, a a^T)^{-1} = I_n + c\, a a^T$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
1. For known $\rho$ with $(\beta, \sigma^2)$ unknown: if it exists, find the minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\beta$ among all linear estimators $\hat\beta = a_1 y_1 + \cdots + a_n y_n$. If it does not exist, justify why not.
2. For known $\beta$ with $(\sigma^2, \rho)$ unknown: find the MLE for $(\sigma^2, \rho)$. Clearly justify why it is the MLE.
3. For $(\beta, \sigma^2, \rho)$ all unknown: (a) Find the minimal sufficient statistic, and find necessary and sufficient conditions on $x_1,\dots,x_n$ for the minimal sufficient statistic to be complete. (b) If they exist, find the MLE for $(\beta, \sigma^2, \rho)$ in the two cases (i) $x_1 = \cdots = x_n$, and (ii) $x_1 + \cdots + x_n = 0$. If the MLE does not exist, justify why not.

Let \(\mathbf 1=(1,\dots,1)^T\), \(J=\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^T\), and let  

\[
P=\frac{J}{n},\qquad Q=I_n-P,\qquad m=n-1.
\]

Thus \(P\) projects onto \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}\), while \(Q\) projects onto the centered subspace. The correlation matrix is

\[
R_\rho=(1-\rho)I_n+\rho J=(1-\rho)Q+\{1+(n-1)\rho\}P.
\]

Its eigenvalues are \(1+(n-1)\rho\) on \(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf 1\}\) and \(1-\rho\) on the centered subspace, so it is positive definite exactly for

\[
-\frac1{n-1}<\rho<1.
\]

Also,

\[
R_\rho^{-1}=\frac1{1-\rho}Q+\frac1{1+(n-1)\rho}P.
\]

It will be useful to reparametrize

\[
\alpha=\sigma^2\{1+(n-1)\rho\},\qquad \gamma=\sigma^2(1-\rho).
\]

Then \((\sigma^2,\rho)\leftrightarrow(\alpha,\gamma)\) is a bijection between the given parameter space and \((0,\infty)^2\), with inverse

\[
\sigma^2=\frac{\alpha+(n-1)\gamma}{n},\qquad 
\rho=\frac{\alpha-\gamma}{\alpha+(n-1)\gamma}.
\]

Let

\[
U=\frac{\mathbf 1^T Y}{\sqrt n},\qquad V=QY,
\]

where \(V\) is regarded in an orthonormal coordinate system for the centered subspace. Similarly define

\[
\xi=\frac{\mathbf 1^T x}{\sqrt n},\qquad \eta=Qx.
\]

Then

\[
U\sim N(\beta \xi,\alpha),\qquad V\sim N(\beta\eta,\gamma I_{n-1}),
\]

and \(U\) and \(V\) are independent.

---

## 1. Known \(\rho\), unknown \((\beta,\sigma^2)\)

A linear estimator has the form \(\widehat\beta=a^T Y\). It is unbiased for \(\beta\) iff

\[
\mathbb E_\beta(a^T Y)=a^T(\beta x)=\beta
\]

for all \(\beta\), i.e.

\[
a^T x=1.
\]

If \(x=0\), no such \(a\) exists, so no unbiased linear estimator exists.

Assume \(x\neq 0\). Then

\[
\operatorname{var}(a^T Y)=\sigma^2 a^T R_\rho a.
\]

We minimize \(a^T R_\rho a\) subject to \(a^T x=1\). By Lagrange multipliers,

\[
2R_\rho a-\lambda x=0,
\]

so

\[
a=\frac{\lambda}{2}R_\rho^{-1}x.
\]

Using \(a^T x=1\),

\[
\frac{\lambda}{2}x^T R_\rho^{-1}x=1,
\]

hence

\[
a=\frac{R_\rho^{-1}x}{x^T R_\rho^{-1}x}.
\]

Therefore the minimum variance unbiased linear estimator is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{GLS}}
=
\frac{x^T R_\rho^{-1}Y}{x^T R_\rho^{-1}x}
}
\]

provided \(x\neq 0\). Its variance is

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{var}(\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{GLS}})
=
\frac{\sigma^2}{x^T R_\rho^{-1}x}.
}
\]

Using the projection form of \(R_\rho^{-1}\),

\[
x^T R_\rho^{-1}x
=
\frac{x^TQx}{1-\rho}
+
\frac{x^TPx}{1+(n-1)\rho}
=
\frac{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)^2}{1-\rho}
+
\frac{(\sum_i x_i)^2/n}{1+(n-1)\rho}.
\]

This is strictly positive when \(x\neq 0\).

---

## 2. Known \(\beta\), unknown \((\sigma^2,\rho)\)

Let

\[
r=Y-\beta x.
\]

Then \(r\sim N(0,\sigma^2R_\rho)\). Define

\[
B=r^TPr=\frac{(\mathbf 1^T r)^2}{n}=n\bar r^2,
\qquad
S=r^TQr=\sum_{i=1}^n (r_i-\bar r)^2.
\]

In the \((\alpha,\gamma)\) parametrization, the likelihood is

\[
L(\alpha,\gamma)
\propto
\alpha^{-1/2}\gamma^{-(n-1)/2}
\exp\left\{-\frac{B}{2\alpha}-\frac{S}{2\gamma}\right\}.
\]

The two factors separate. For \(t>0\),

\[
\ell(t)=-\frac{k}{2}\log t-\frac{s}{2t}
\]

is maximized at \(t=s/k\) if \(s>0\). If \(s=0\), the likelihood is unbounded as \(t\downarrow 0\).

Thus a finite MLE exists iff

\[
B>0\quad\text{and}\quad S>0.
\]

When this holds,

\[
\widehat\alpha=B,\qquad \widehat\gamma=\frac{S}{n-1}.
\]

Transforming back,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat{\sigma}^2
=
\frac{B+S}{n}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n r_i^2
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{B-\frac{S}{n-1}}{B+S}.
}
\]

If \(B=0\) or \(S=0\), the likelihood is unbounded at the boundary of the parameter space, so no MLE exists.

---

## 3(a). All parameters unknown: minimal sufficiency and completeness

Recall

\[
U=\frac{\mathbf 1^T Y}{\sqrt n},\qquad V=QY,
\]

and

\[
\xi=\frac{\mathbf 1^T x}{\sqrt n},\qquad \eta=Qx.
\]

The joint density in \((U,V)\) is

\[
f_{\beta,\alpha,\gamma}(u,v)
\propto
\alpha^{-1/2}\gamma^{-(n-1)/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(u-\beta\xi)^2}{2\alpha}
-\frac{\|v-\beta\eta\|^2}{2\gamma}
\right\}.
\]

For two observations \((u,v)\) and \((u',v')\), the likelihood ratio is parameter-free iff

\[
(u-\beta\xi)^2-(u'-\beta\xi)^2=0
\]

and

\[
\|v-\beta\eta\|^2-\|v'-\beta\eta\|^2=0
\]

for every \(\beta\). Equivalently,

\[
u^2=u'^2,\qquad \xi(u-u')=0,
\]

and

\[
\|v\|^2=\|v'\|^2,\qquad \eta^T(v-v')=0.
\]

By the Lehmann–Scheffé minimal sufficiency criterion, a minimal sufficient statistic is therefore

\[
\boxed{
T(Y)=
\begin{cases}
\left(U,\ \eta^T V,\ \|V\|^2\right), & \xi\neq 0,\ \eta\neq 0,\\[4pt]
\left(U,\ \|V\|^2\right), & \xi\neq 0,\ \eta=0,\\[4pt]
\left(U^2,\ \eta^T V,\ \|V\|^2\right), & \xi=0,\ \eta\neq 0,\\[4pt]
\left(U^2,\ \|V\|^2\right), & \xi=0,\ \eta=0.
\end{cases}
}
\]

In original coordinates,

\[
U=\frac{\sum_i Y_i}{\sqrt n},
\qquad
\|V\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-\bar Y)^2,
\]

and

\[
\eta^T V=(Qx)^T(QY)=\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y).
\]

Now,

\[
\xi=0 \Longleftrightarrow \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0,
\]

and

\[
\eta=0 \Longleftrightarrow x_1=\cdots=x_n.
\]

The statistic \(T\) is complete iff

\[
\boxed{
\xi=0\ \text{or}\ \eta=0
}
\]

i.e. iff

\[
\boxed{
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0
\quad\text{or}\quad
x_1=\cdots=x_n.
}
\]

Indeed, if both \(\xi\neq 0\) and \(\eta\neq 0\), then

\[
g(T)=\frac{\eta^T V}{\|\eta\|^2}-\frac{U}{\xi}
\]

is a nonzero statistic with

\[
\mathbb E_{\beta,\alpha,\gamma}[g(T)]
=
\beta-\beta
=
0
\]

for all parameter values, so \(T\) is not complete.

Conversely, if \(\xi=0\) or \(\eta=0\), completeness follows from the standard completeness of the normal location family and the gamma scale family, together with independence of the \(P\)- and \(Q\)-components.

---

## 3(b). MLEs when all parameters are unknown

Use the \((\alpha,\gamma)\) parametrization. Recall

\[
\sigma^2=\frac{\alpha+(n-1)\gamma}{n},
\qquad
\rho=\frac{\alpha-\gamma}{\alpha+(n-1)\gamma}.
\]

Let

\[
u=\frac{\mathbf 1^T y}{\sqrt n},
\qquad
S=y^TQy=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2.
\]

---

### Case (i): \(x_1=\cdots=x_n=c\)

Then \(\eta=0\) and \(\xi=\sqrt n\,c\). The likelihood is

\[
L(\beta,\alpha,\gamma)
\propto
\alpha^{-1/2}\gamma^{-(n-1)/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(u-\beta\xi)^2}{2\alpha}
-\frac{S}{2\gamma}
\right\}.
\]

If \(c\neq 0\), then \(\xi\neq 0\). Choosing

\[
\beta=\frac{u}{\xi}
\]

makes the \(U\)-residual exactly zero. Then letting \(\alpha\downarrow 0\) sends the likelihood to \(+\infty\). Hence:

\[
\boxed{
\text{If }c\neq 0,\text{ no MLE exists.}
}
\]

If \(c=0\), then \(x=0\) and \(\beta\) is not identifiable. The likelihood becomes

\[
L(\alpha,\gamma)
\propto
\alpha^{-1/2}\gamma^{-(n-1)/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{u^2}{2\alpha}
-\frac{S}{2\gamma}
\right\}.
\]

A finite maximum exists iff

\[
u^2>0
\quad\text{and}\quad
S>0.
\]

When this holds,

\[
\widehat\alpha=u^2,
\qquad
\widehat\gamma=\frac{S}{n-1}.
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{u^2+S}{n}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{u^2-\frac{S}{n-1}}{u^2+S}.
}
\]

Since \(\beta\) is not identifiable, every \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) is an MLE. If \(u=0\) or \(S=0\), the likelihood is unbounded and no MLE exists.

---

### Case (ii): \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=0\)

Then \(\xi=0\), so the likelihood is

\[
L(\beta,\alpha,\gamma)
\propto
\alpha^{-1/2}\gamma^{-(n-1)/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{u^2}{2\alpha}
-\frac{\|Qy-\beta x\|^2}{2\gamma}
\right\}.
\]

First suppose \(x\neq 0\). Then

\[
\widehat\beta
=
\frac{x^T y}{x^T x}.
\]

Let

\[
\operatorname{RSS}
=
\|Qy-\widehat\beta x\|^2
=
y^TQy-\frac{(x^T y)^2}{x^T x}.
\]

A finite MLE exists iff

\[
u^2>0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{RSS}>0.
\]

When this holds,

\[
\widehat\alpha=u^2,
\qquad
\widehat\gamma=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta=\frac{x^T y}{x^T x}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{u^2+\operatorname{RSS}}{n}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{u^2-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-1}}{u^2+\operatorname{RSS}}.
}
\]

If \(u=0\), the likelihood is unbounded as \(\alpha\downarrow 0\). If \(\operatorname{RSS}=0\), the likelihood is unbounded as \(\gamma\downarrow 0\). Hence no MLE exists in either case.

If \(x=0\), this reduces to the \(c=0\) subcase from case (i): \(\beta\) is arbitrary, and the MLE for \((\sigma^2,\rho)\) exists iff \(u^2>0\) and \(S>0\), with

\[
\widehat\sigma^2=\frac{u^2+S}{n},
\qquad
\widehat\rho=\frac{u^2-\frac{S}{n-1}}{u^2+S}.
\]

\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{RSS}>0.
\]

When this holds,

\[
\widehat\alpha=u^2,
\qquad
\widehat\gamma=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-1}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta=\frac{x^T y}{x^T x}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\sigma^2
=
\frac{u^2+\operatorname{RSS}}{n}
}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\rho
=
\frac{u^2-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-1}}{u^2+\operatorname{RSS}}.
}
\]

If \(u=0\), the likelihood is unbounded as \(\alpha\downarrow 0\). If \(\operatorname{RSS}=0\), the likelihood is unbounded as \(\gamma\downarrow 0\). Hence no MLE exists in either case.

If \(x=0\), this reduces to the \(c=0\) subcase from case (i): \(\beta\) is arbitrary, and the MLE for \((\sigma^2,\rho)\) exists iff \(u^2>0\) and \(S>0\), with

\[
\widehat\sigma^2=\frac{u^2+S}{n},
\qquad
\widehat\rho=\frac{u^2-\frac{S}{n-1}}{u^2+S}.
\]
